---
title: "Recursive Counting Across Scale"
subtitle: "Each boundary counts a different object"
toc: true
---

R<sup>2</sup>D is not simply a theory of counting states within one boundary.

It is a theory of what happens when **count domains are recursively nested**.

At one boundary, a distinction is readable as a state.

At another boundary, that state no longer retains the same count identity.

A completed local relation can instead participate in the realization of an
enclosing state.

The pattern can then repeat.

This gives the primitive architecture:

$$
\boxed{
B_{n-1}
\rightarrow
B_n
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}
\rightarrow
B_{n+2}
\rightarrow
\cdots
}
$$

But the arrows do not mean that one unchanged object simply moves upward
through larger containers.

At every boundary:

> **the count domain changes, the state domain changes, and the identity of
> what is being counted changes.**

That is recursive counting.

## Each Boundary Has Its Own States

At boundary $B_n$, the readable macrostate domain is

$$
\mathcal M_n.
$$

Its formal microstates belong to

$$
\mathfrak M_n.
$$

The classification map

$$
\pi_n:
\mathfrak M_n
\rightarrow
\mathcal M_n
$$

defines the multiplicity

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\left|
\pi_n^{-1}(i)
\right|.
$$

Move to $B_{n+1}$, and a new classification is defined.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal M_n
\not\equiv
\mathcal M_{n+1}.
}
$$

The enclosing boundary does not simply inherit the same state space with less
detail.

It counts something new.

[Macrostate and Microstate →](macrostate-microstate.qmd)

## Recursive Replacement Comes Before Recursive Counting

Because state identity is boundary relative, changing the count boundary
produces **recursive replacement**.

A state readable at $B_n$ does not persist unchanged as a state of
$B_{n+1}$.

Instead,

$$
\boxed{
\text{state domain at } B_n
\rightarrow
\text{boundary change}
\rightarrow
\text{new state domain at } B_{n+1}.
}
$$

The subordinate relation can remain consequential.

Its local state identity does not.

This is why recursion in R<sup>2</sup>D is not simply a stack of persistent
objects.

[Recursive Replacement →](recursive-replacement.qmd)

## Completion Creates Something New to Count

Suppose a readable path at $B_n$ completes a closure:

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}:
i
\rightarrow
k
\rightarrow
i.
$$

At $B_n$, the internal path is readable.

Once completed, that relation can be classified from the enclosing boundary.

Recursive carry expresses this as

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
}
$$

The closure has not physically transformed into the enclosing occurrence.

Its **count meaning has changed**.

This is the basic recursive operation:

> **A completed relation at one boundary becomes countable under a new
> classification at the next.**

[Recursive Carry →](recursive-carry.qmd)

## The Count Does Not Preserve the Internal Sequence

This provides a useful way to distinguish physical recursive counting from
ordinary positional counting.

In ordinary base-ten notation, a digit moves through a prescribed sequence:

$$
0,1,2,\ldots,9,
$$

and then carries to the next position.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not require a physical state path to traverse a prescribed
sequence.

A closure might instead be

$$
A
\rightarrow
B
\rightarrow
D
\rightarrow
A,
$$

or

$$
0
\rightarrow
3
\rightarrow
6
\rightarrow
0.
$$

What matters for recursive counting is not the particular ordering of the
intermediate labels.

What matters is that the relation becomes distinguishably complete relative
to its boundary and can then acquire a new count meaning at the enclosing
boundary.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{internal path}
\rightarrow
\text{completion}
\rightarrow
\text{enclosing classification}.
}
$$

The enclosing boundary need not preserve the full sequence in order to count
its consequence.

## The Base Changes With the Boundary

Ordinary positional counting uses a fixed base.

R<sup>2</sup>D does not assume one universal base.

The available state domain is defined by the boundary itself.

At one boundary there may be two readable states.

At another there may be eleven.

At another there may be an entirely different multiplicity landscape.

So the recursive operation is not

$$
\text{same base}
+
\text{larger number}.
$$

It is

$$
\boxed{
\text{new boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{new state domain}
\rightarrow
\text{new count structure}.
}
$$

This is another reason scale change in R<sup>2</sup>D is stronger than
ordinary coarse-graining.

## Coins Make the Recursion Concrete

Begin with one coin boundary.

Its readable states are

$$
H
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
T.
$$

Now let ten peer coin boundaries define one ensemble boundary.

The ensemble does not possess twenty macrostates corresponding to ten copies
of $H$ and $T$.

Instead, it defines a new eleven-state macrostate domain:

$$
N_H
=
0,1,2,\ldots,10.
$$

Its multiplicity landscape is

$$
W_{n,i}
=
\binom{10}{i}.
$$

So:

$$
\boxed{
10\text{ two-state boundaries}
\rightarrow
1\text{ eleven-state landscape}.
}
$$

The subordinate binary domains have been recursively replaced by a new
whole-system classification.

[The Coins Example →](coins.qmd)

## The Next Boundary Counts Landscapes, Not Restored Coins

Now suppose the next boundary contains ten such ensemble boundaries.

The crucial point is that $B_{n+1}$ does **not** return to the lower
description and treat one hundred individual $H/T$ identities as its
primitive states.

It counts ten already-defined $B_n$ landscapes.

Schematically:

$$
\boxed{
\underbrace{
B_n,\,
B_n,\,
\dots,\,
B_n
}_{10\ \text{peer landscapes}}
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}.
}
$$

A closed-form calculation may ultimately reproduce a familiar combinatorial
result associated with one hundred binary elements.

But that mathematical equivalence does not restore the one hundred
lower-boundary identities as the primitive state variables at $B_{n+1}$.

This is the distinction between:

$$
\boxed{
\text{recursive count consequence}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\text{persistence of subordinate state identity}.
}
$$

They are not the same claim.

## Compatible Possibilities Multiply

The recursive structure retains the primitive counting rules introduced
earlier.

For compatible peer multiplicities,

$$
W_1,W_2,\ldots,W_m,
$$

the joint possible count is

$$
\boxed{
W_{\mathrm{joint}}
=
\prod_{\alpha=1}^{m}W_\alpha.
}
$$

Taking logarithms gives

$$
\boxed{
\ln W_{\mathrm{joint}}
=
\sum_{\alpha=1}^{m}\ln W_\alpha.
}
$$

Thus multiplicative count composition becomes additive in logarithmic
coordinates.

At the same time, mutually exclusive macrostate alternatives within one
boundary add:

$$
\Theta_n
=
\sum_{i\in\mathcal M_n}
W_{n,i}.
$$

So recursive counting is built from two primitive operations:

> **Compatible possibilities multiply.**

> **Mutually exclusive alternatives add.**

[Counting Requires Distinguishability →](counting.qmd)

## Recursion Is Not Bottom-Up Causation

The direction of counting must not be confused with the direction of causal
organization.

Recursive carry can be written

$$
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}.
$$

This looks upward.

But the arrow means **reclassification**, not causation.

Causally, the enclosing occurrence defines which local realizations are
compatible with it:

$$
\boxed{
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
\Longrightarrow
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}.
}
$$

Thus two complementary relations coexist:

$$
\boxed{
\text{enclosing organization}
\Longrightarrow
\text{local realization}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\text{completed local realization}
\xmapsto{\text{boundary change}}
\text{enclosing count meaning}.
}
$$

Recursive counting therefore does not require smaller things to build larger
things causally.

[The Causal Inversion →](causal-inversion.qmd)

## Recurrence Supplies the Across-Boundary Count

Once a local closure is complete, it can recur.

Within a common recurrence-comparison domain $\mathcal D_R$, let

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
$$

count completed local closure recurrences.

Let

$$
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
$$

count corresponding enclosing recurrences.

The adjacent recurrence ratio is

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\frac{
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\chi_{n+1}
\right)
}{
N_{\mathcal D_R}
\left(
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\right)
}.
}
$$

This ratio tells us how recursive realization scales from one boundary to the
next.

[Recurrence →](recurrence.qmd)

## Recurrence Ratios Compose Multiplicatively

Now consider a chain

$$
B_n
\rightarrow
B_{n+1}
\rightarrow
B_{n+2}
\rightarrow
\cdots
\rightarrow
B_N.
$$

The adjacent recurrence ratios are

$$
\rho_{n+1|n},
\quad
\rho_{n+2|n+1},
\quad
\dots,
\quad
\rho_{N|N-1}.
$$

If the same recurrence-comparison domain jointly counts the boundaries in
the chain, the ratios compose multiplicatively:

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{N|n}
=
\prod_{j=n}^{N-1}
\rho_{j+1|j}.
}
$$

The intermediate recurrence counts cancel.

This is the recursive analogue of telescoping ratios.

## Logarithms Turn Recursive Scaling Into Addition

Define the adjacent logarithmic recurrence scaling

$$
\gamma_{j+1|j}
=
\ln\rho_{j+1|j}.
$$

Then the accumulated recurrence scaling from $B_n$ to $B_N$ is

$$
\boxed{
\Gamma_{N|n}
=
\sum_{j=n}^{N-1}
\ln\rho_{j+1|j}.
}
$$

Equivalently,

$$
\boxed{
\Gamma_{N|n}
=
\ln\rho_{N|n}.
}
$$

Again, multiplicative recursive composition becomes additive in logarithmic
coordinates.

This is the same mathematical architecture already encountered with
multiplicity.

## Distinguishability Also Scales Across Boundaries

Recurrence is only one aspect of the recursive relation.

A readable transition at boundary $B_j$ also has a distinguishable interval

$$
\lambda_j.
$$

For a reference boundary $B_n$ and a larger boundary $B_N$, define the
accumulated distinguishability scaling

$$
\boxed{
\Lambda_{N|n}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
|\lambda_N|
}{
|\lambda_n|
}
\right).
}
$$

This asks how the readable distinguishable interval changes across the same
recursive hierarchy.

Thus recursive comparison contains two independent scale relations:

$$
\boxed{
\Lambda
=
\text{distinguishability scaling}
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\Gamma
=
\text{recurrence scaling}.
}
$$

Neither is yet space or time.

## Two Coordinates of Recursive Readability

This gives R<sup>2</sup>D two primitive aspects of recursive closure.

One asks:

> **How does distinguishability change across boundaries?**

The other asks:

> **How does recurrence change across boundaries?**

These are quantified by

$$
\Lambda_{N|n}
$$

and

$$
\Gamma_{N|n}.
$$

Their accumulated difference can be written

$$
\boxed{
H_{N|n}
=
\Lambda_{N|n}
-
\Gamma_{N|n}.
}
$$

or

$$
\boxed{
H_{N|n}
=
\ln
\left[
\frac{
|\lambda_N|/|\lambda_n|
}{
\displaystyle
\prod_{j=n}^{N-1}
\rho_{j+1|j}
}
\right].
}
$$

This quantity is not a third primitive coordinate.

It measures the relative accumulated scaling of the two.

## Recursive Scale Exists Before Spatial Scale

The index

$$
n
$$

should not automatically be read as spatial size.

A larger boundary is a more enclosing **count domain**.

Physical size may later correlate with that hierarchy in a particular
mapping.

But the primitive recursion requires only:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary nesting}
+
\text{state replacement}
+
\text{recursive recurrence}.
}
$$

Thus R<sup>2</sup>D defines a notion of scale before meters, seconds, or
spacetime coordinates have been introduced.

This is why Part I is a theory of **dimensionless recursive counting**.

## The Recursive Clock

The recurrence hierarchy provides a useful intuition.

Imagine each boundary as a gear.

The local closure is the gear's readable cycle.

Its distinguishable interval is associated with

$$
\lambda_n.
$$

Its recurrence relative to adjacent boundaries is associated with

$$
\rho_{n+1|n}.
$$

Smaller boundaries can complete many local recurrences while an enclosing
boundary completes only one—or none within the same comparison domain.

The smaller gear therefore appears active.

The larger gear may appear nearly motionless.

But rapid local recurrence does not imply causal priority.

The smaller gear realizes the recursively organized relation.

It does not independently create the enclosing relation.

## What Looks Static May Still Organize

Suppose

$$
\rho_{n+1|n}
\ll1.
$$

Many local closures occur for one enclosing recurrence.

Over a finite observation domain, the enclosing boundary may not visibly
recur at all:

$$
\rho_{n+1|n}=0
$$

within that domain.

But its compatibility relation can still define which subordinate
realizations belong to the enclosing state.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\text{unresolved enclosing recurrence}
\neq
\text{absence of enclosing organization}.
}
$$

This becomes essential when R<sup>2</sup>D later considers readability
horizons.

## Recursive Counting Can Outrun Joint Readability

As recursive scaling accumulates, distinguishability and recurrence need not
remain equally readable.

If distinguishability becomes dominant relative to recurrence,

$$
H_{N|n}
\rightarrow
+\infty,
$$

the recursive hierarchy approaches a distinguishability-dominant limit.

If recurrence becomes dominant relative to distinguishability,

$$
H_{N|n}
\rightarrow
-\infty,
$$

it approaches the opposite limit.

But a large mathematical imbalance alone is not yet a horizon.

A readability horizon appears only when one relation actually becomes
unresolvable while the other remains readable.

Between those limits, both can remain jointly readable.

This later produces the two opposite readability horizons developed in the
Canon.

## Occurrence Is Still Separate

It is important not to confuse accumulated recurrence scaling

$$
\Gamma
$$

with the within-boundary occurrence coordinate

$$
\tau_{n,i}
=
\ln\nu_{n,i}.
$$

Likewise, closure nonreciprocity

$$
L_{\tau,n,\alpha,\mathcal C}
$$

does not define the recurrence scaling.

These belong to different count relations.

Occurrence asks how realization is distributed **within a boundary**.

Recurrence scaling compares completed realization **across boundaries**.

Thus:

$$
\boxed{
\tau
\neq
\Gamma.
}
$$

## Background Is Also Separate

The R<sup>2</sup>D Second Law later relates local nonreciprocal
occurrence-count realization to an enclosing nondirectional background
increment.

That relation is distinct from the recursive scaling coordinates

$$
\Lambda
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\Gamma.
$$

Background therefore does not create a third recursive scale coordinate.

Recursive geometry remains organized around the relation between
distinguishability and recurrence.

[The R²D Second Law →](second-law.qmd)

## Recursive Counting Before Spacetime

At this stage nothing requires:

- physical distance;
- elapsed time;
- energy;
- force;
- matter;
- particles;
- fields;
- or spacetime.

The primitive architecture is already sufficient to define:

$$
\text{boundary},
$$

$$
\text{state},
$$

$$
\text{multiplicity},
$$

$$
\text{occurrence},
$$

$$
\text{closure},
$$

$$
\text{recurrence},
$$

and

$$
\text{recursive scaling}.
$$

A later physical theory can assign familiar coordinates to those relations.

But those coordinates are readings of a structure that has already been
defined.

## Why Recursive Counting Matters

The full inversion can now be seen.

Conventional science often begins with physical objects distributed through
space and evolving through time.

R<sup>2</sup>D begins instead with:

$$
\boxed{
\text{boundary}
\rightarrow
\text{distinction}
\rightarrow
\text{multiplicity}
\rightarrow
\text{realization}
\rightarrow
\text{closure}
\rightarrow
\text{recurrence}
\rightarrow
\text{recursive replacement}.
}
$$

Only afterward does it ask how familiar physical coordinates read that
structure.

Thus:

> **Scale is first a relation among count boundaries.**

> **Time is first approached through recurrence.**

> **Geometry is first approached through distinguishability.**

The familiar physical ontology comes later.

## The Architecture in One Diagram

The recursive architecture can be summarized as

$$
\boxed{
\begin{array}{ccccc}
B_n
&
\longrightarrow
&
B_{n+1}
&
\longrightarrow
&
B_{n+2}
\\[6pt]

\mathcal C_n
&
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
&
\chi_{n+1}
&
\xmapsto{\kappa_{n+1}}
&
\chi_{n+2}
\\[6pt]

\lambda_n
&
\longrightarrow
&
\lambda_{n+1}
&
\longrightarrow
&
\lambda_{n+2}
\\[6pt]

N_n
&
\xrightarrow{\rho_{n+1|n}}
&
N_{n+1}
&
\xrightarrow{\rho_{n+2|n+1}}
&
N_{n+2}
\end{array}
}
$$

The first row changes the count boundary.

The second changes the classification of completed realization.

The third tracks distinguishability.

The fourth tracks recurrence.

Together they define recursive count structure.

## Core Equations

### Recursive carry

$$
\boxed{
\mathcal C_{n,\alpha}
\xmapsto{\kappa_n}
\chi_{n+1}^{(r)}
}
$$

### Adjacent recurrence ratio

$$
\boxed{
\rho_{n+1|n,\alpha}
=
\frac{
N_{\mathcal D_R}(\chi_{n+1})
}{
N_{\mathcal D_R}(\mathcal C_{n,\alpha})
}
}
$$

### Accumulated recurrence scaling

$$
\boxed{
\Gamma_{N|n}
=
\sum_{j=n}^{N-1}
\ln\rho_{j+1|j}
}
$$

### Accumulated distinguishability scaling

$$
\boxed{
\Lambda_{N|n}
=
\ln
\left(
\frac{
|\lambda_N|
}{
|\lambda_n|
}
\right)
}
$$

### Relative accumulated scaling

$$
\boxed{
H_{N|n}
=
\Lambda_{N|n}
-
\Gamma_{N|n}
}
$$

---

## The Key Distinction

The simplest summary is:

> **A boundary counts states.**

> **A completed state relation can itself become countable at an enclosing
> boundary.**

> **The enclosing boundary replaces the subordinate state domain rather than
> preserving it unchanged.**

> **Repeating this operation creates a hierarchy of recursively related count
> domains.**

Across that hierarchy, distinguishability and recurrence scale separately.

That is the mathematical structure the R<sup>2</sup>D law now connects.
